intro.text:
In the heart of Hanoi, there is an alley with a very special name: Cấm Chỉ.

Folk tales say the name is linked to Chúa Chổm, who later became King Lê Trang Tông. In his humble early days, he often ate on credit at food stalls. When he was welcomed back to become king, many of his old creditors came, pointing and demanding payment.

Legend has it that an order of prohibition was issued, and from then on people called this place Cấm Chỉ.

It is an anecdote that has not been verified as a historical event, but it remains an engaging story tied to the name of the alley.

Today, Cấm Chỉ no longer suggests prohibition. On the contrary, it welcomes diners with eateries, lights, and the rhythm of food life in the Old Quarter.

alleyStory.title: Cấm Chỉ Alley
paragraphs: Cấm Chỉ Alley is linked to a well-known folk anecdote about Chúa Chổm, often associated with King Lê Trang Tông.

According to the story recorded by VOV Giao thông (2025), when Chúa Chổm was in humble circumstances, he often ate on credit at food stalls. When Nguyễn Kim found him and established him as king, he passed through this area and old creditors pointed him out and demanded payment. According to legend, the order “Cấm Chỉ” was issued to stop people from pointing at the king to demand debts.

However, this is a folk anecdote, not a historical event that has been fully verified. VOV Giao thông (2025) also mentions another explanation: the name relates to an area where officials and troops passed and ordinary people had limited access.

Today, Cấm Chỉ and Tống Duy Tân Street form a long-standing food district. Food businesses here were organized and the area was refurbished beginning in the early 2000s. In early 2025, the area was further renovated, adding a public art space with an entrance arch and a statue of a pho vendor (Hà Nội Online, 2025; VnExpress, 2001).
Distinctive character: A name linked to folk legend, alongside a late-night food district and public art.

eat.name: Bánh cuốn Kỳ Đồng
eat.dishes: Steamed rice rolls, chả quế, fried shallots, and shrimp floss.
eat.hours: Reference hours: 07:00–21:00 in current directories; VnExpress (2020) listed 07:00–23:00.

eat.name: Xôi Hồng
eat.dishes: Xôi xéo, chicken sticky rice, and other savory sticky-rice dishes.
eat.note: No reliable hours have been confirmed.

eat.name: Gà tần Cây Si
eat.dishes: Herbal chicken stew, chicken-stew noodles, and honey bread.
eat.hours: Reference hours: 08:30–22:30 according to a directory.

eat.name: Lẩu Thắng Béo
eat.dishes: Frog hotpot, Thai-style hotpot, and dishes for sharing.
eat.hours: Reference hours: 17:00–05:00 the next day according to a directory; confirm if visiting late at night.

visit.name: Tống Duy Tân Public Art Space
notes: View the entrance arch inspired by the Đại Hưng Gate of the old citadel.
Learn about the pho-vendor statue and the story of how the food district developed.
The space was refurbished and introduced to the public in January 2025 (Hà Nội Online, 2025).

visit.name: Hội Vũ Alley
notes: The alley connects Hàng Bông, Quán Sứ, and Tràng Thi streets.
It is noted for its older architecture and stories about residents, including the businesswoman Cô Tư Hồng.
It can be chosen to broaden an exploration of urban life and history (VOV Giao thông, 2025b).

visit.name: Vọng Tiên Temple
notes: You can combine a visit with learning about local religious spaces and folklore.
Visit only during hours and under conditions permitted by the site manager.

route: Tống Duy Tân Public Art Space
Bánh cuốn or herbal chicken stew
caveats: VnExpress (2020) featured Bánh cuốn Kỳ Đồng, chicken-stew shops, and hotpot in the area. Prices in a 2020 article should not be treated as current.
